courses.title: Bhagavad Gita: The Essence, Chapter by Chapter
courses.subtitle: Short, clear lessons on the teachings Krishna gave Arjuna on the battlefield of Kurukshetra.
courses.description:
The Bhagavad Gita is 700 verses in 18 chapters, set inside the Mahabharata. This series walks through its core ideas in plain language, a few chapters at a time.

## What you'll learn

- Why Arjuna lays down his bow, and what Krishna tells him
- Karma Yoga: acting without attachment to results
- Jnana, Bhakti and Dhyana: the paths of knowledge, devotion and meditation
- How these ideas apply to everyday decisions

lessons.title: Arjuna's dilemma (Chapter 1)
lessons.summary: On the battlefield, Arjuna sees his teachers and relatives on the other side and cannot fight.
lessons.content:
The Gita opens with the blind king **Dhritarashtra** asking his charioteer **Sanjaya** what is happening at Kurukshetra.

Arjuna asks Krishna, his charioteer, to drive between the two armies. Seeing his grandsire Bhishma, his teacher Drona and his cousins ready for war, he is overwhelmed with grief. He puts down his bow, Gandiva, and says he would rather not fight.

> Chapter 1 is called *Arjuna Vishada Yoga*, the yoga of Arjuna's despair.

### Reflection

Everyone meets moments where duty and emotion pull in opposite directions. The Gita begins with that confusion, not with answers.

lessons.title: The eternal self (Chapter 2)
lessons.summary: Krishna teaches that the soul (atman) is never born and never dies.
lessons.content:
Chapter 2, *Sankhya Yoga*, is often called the summary of the whole Gita.

## The atman

Krishna explains that the true self is eternal. Just as a person discards worn-out clothes and puts on new ones, the soul leaves a worn-out body and takes a new one (2.22).

## Your right is to action

> कर्मण्येवाधिकारस्ते मा फलेषु कदाचन ।
>
> *Karmaṇy-evādhikāras te mā phaleṣhu kadāchana* (2.47)

You have a right to your actions, but never to their fruits. Don't let the results be your motive, and don't be attached to inaction either.

## Sthitaprajna

The chapter ends by describing the *sthitaprajna*, a person of steady wisdom, who is not shaken by pleasure or pain.

lessons.title: Karma Yoga: the path of action (Chapter 3)
lessons.summary: Why no one can stay without acting, and how to act without attachment.
lessons.content:
Arjuna asks: if knowledge is better than action, why push me into this terrible war?

Krishna answers that nobody can remain without action even for a moment; nature makes everyone act (3.5). The question is *how* to act.

## Yajna: action as offering

Work done as an offering, for the welfare of all and not for selfish gain, does not bind a person (3.9).

## Lead by example

> Whatever a great person does, others follow. Whatever standard they set, the world pursues. (3.21)

### Practice

Pick one routine task today and do it fully, as an offering, without worrying about praise or reward.

lessons.title: Bhakti: the path of devotion (Chapter 12)
lessons.summary: Krishna describes the qualities of a devotee who is dear to him.
lessons.content:
Arjuna asks who is better: those who worship the formless, or those who worship God with form. Krishna says both reach him, but devotion to the personal form is easier for embodied beings.

## Qualities of a dear devotee (12.13–12.19)

- Free from hatred, friendly and compassionate to all
- Free from possessiveness and ego
- Equal in pleasure and pain, forgiving
- Content, self-controlled and firm in resolve
- Not disturbing the world, and not disturbed by it

Chapter 12 is one of the shortest chapters, only 20 verses, and is often recited daily.

posts.title: The Meaning of the Gayatri Mantra
posts.excerpt: One of the oldest and most revered mantras, from the Rig Veda. Here is what each line means.
posts.content:
The Gayatri Mantra comes from the **Rig Veda (3.62.10)** and is addressed to **Savitr**, the divine light of the Sun.

> ॐ भूर्भुवः स्वः ।
> तत्सवितुर्वरेण्यं ।
> भर्गो देवस्य धीमहि ।
> धियो यो नः प्रचोदयात् ॥

*Om bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ, tat savitur vareṇyaṃ, bhargo devasya dhīmahi, dhiyo yo naḥ prachodayāt.*

## Line by line

| Words | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Om bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ | Om. Earth, atmosphere and the heavens |
| Tat savitur vareṇyaṃ | That most excellent light of Savitr |
| Bhargo devasya dhīmahi | We meditate on the radiance of the divine |
| Dhiyo yo naḥ prachodayāt | May it inspire our understanding |

## When to chant

Traditionally at the three *sandhyas*: dawn, noon and dusk. Many people chant it 3, 11 or 108 times.

posts.title: Ekadashi: Why the 11th Day Is Special
posts.excerpt: Twice every lunar month, devotees of Vishnu fast on Ekadashi. Here's the meaning and how the fast is kept.
posts.content:
**Ekadashi** is the 11th tithi of each paksha, so it comes twice a lunar month: once in Shukla paksha (waxing) and once in Krishna paksha (waning). That makes 24 Ekadashis a year, and 26 in a year with an extra month (Adhik Maas).

## Why fast?

Ekadashi is dedicated to **Lord Vishnu**. The Padma Purana describes Ekadashi as a goddess born from Vishnu, and fasting on this day is believed to purify the mind and body.

## How the fast is kept

- **Nirjala**: no food or water (the strictest form)
- **Phalahar**: fruits, milk and nuts only
- Most traditions avoid grains and beans on Ekadashi.

The fast is broken the next day (Dwadashi) within a set window called *parana*.

## Important Ekadashis

- **Nirjala Ekadashi** (Jyeshtha Shukla)
- **Devshayani Ekadashi** (Ashadha Shukla): Vishnu begins his four-month sleep
- **Prabodhini / Dev Uthani Ekadashi** (Kartik Shukla): Vishnu awakens
- **Vaikuntha Ekadashi** (Margashirsha / Pausha Shukla)

*Check the Panchang on AstroAura for the exact tithi times at your location.*

posts.title: Why We Light a Diya
posts.excerpt: The small oil lamp is part of nearly every Hindu ritual. Its symbolism is simple and beautiful.
posts.content:
A **diya** is a small lamp, traditionally of clay, filled with ghee or oil, with a cotton wick.

## What it represents

- **Light over darkness**: knowledge removing ignorance
- **The ghee or oil**: our tendencies (vasanas), slowly burned away
- **The wick**: the ego, consumed as the light shines
- **The flame always rising upward**: the mind turned towards the higher

## A prayer for lighting the lamp

> शुभं करोति कल्याणमारोग्यं धनसंपदा ।
> शत्रुबुद्धिविनाशाय दीपज्योतिर्नमोऽस्तुते ॥

*I bow to the light of the lamp, which brings auspiciousness, health and prosperity, and destroys hostile thoughts.*

## Simple tips

- Light it at dawn and dusk.
- Use ghee for puja, sesame oil for Shani and Hanuman worship.
- Keep the flame steady and never blow it out; let it go out by itself or extend it with a flower.

posts.title: The 12 Jyotirlingas of Lord Shiva
posts.excerpt: Twelve sacred shrines where Shiva is worshipped as a column of light. Here's where they are.
posts.content:
A **Jyotirlinga** is a shrine where Shiva is worshipped as an endless pillar of light (*jyoti*). The twelve are listed in the *Dwadasha Jyotirlinga Stotram*.

| # | Jyotirlinga | Location |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Somnath | Gujarat |
| 2 | Mallikarjuna | Srisailam, Andhra Pradesh |
| 3 | Mahakaleshwar | Ujjain, Madhya Pradesh |
| 4 | Omkareshwar | Madhya Pradesh |
| 5 | Kedarnath | Uttarakhand |
| 6 | Bhimashankar | Maharashtra |
| 7 | Kashi Vishwanath | Varanasi, Uttar Pradesh |
| 8 | Trimbakeshwar | Nashik, Maharashtra |
| 9 | Baidyanath | Deoghar, Jharkhand |
| 10 | Nageshwar | Dwarka, Gujarat |
| 11 | Rameshwaram | Tamil Nadu |
| 12 | Grishneshwar | Ellora, Maharashtra |

*Some traditions place Baidyanath at Parli (Maharashtra) and Nageshwar near Almora (Uttarakhand).*

## The story

The Shiva Purana tells how Brahma and Vishnu argued over who was supreme. Shiva appeared as an endless column of light and asked them to find its ends. Neither could, and the column became the first Jyotirlinga.
